I commented at the time that the government is buying prohibitionist propaganda disguised as news and/or entertainment. The media are switching from promiscuity to prostitution.

THE SALON SCOOP THAT ALMOST DIDN'T HAPPEN
See
Online Magazine Salon.com Documents Hollywood Sell-Out To Drug Czar

Reporter Dan Forbes waited a year for things to unfold.

Salon.com scored a big scoop last week, landing the San Francisco Internet site on front pages everywhere, but it almost didn't happen.

Salon broke the story that the major television networks were letting censors from the White House drug czar's office fiddle with their prime-time scripts. If a show helped promote an anti-drug message, the network would be relieved of having to air some public service announcements - freeing up that airtime for advertising. The revelations have caused a national furor.

In a way, Salon lucked into the story. It was mid-December, Salon had just moved into its spacious new offices at Fourth and Market streets, boxes were piled everywhere and editors were overloaded trying to keep up with news. Features editor Bill Wyman was told
that someone on the phone wanted to pitch him a story, and Wyman said, " Tell him to e-mail it to us.''

The writer called back two more times, and finally Wyman thought, " Maybe I should talk to the guy.''

It was Dan Forbes, a free-lance writer in New York. He didn't have e-mail. But he did have an amazing story.

Forbes, 43, had spent most of his career writing for trade journals, which is where the story " Prime Time Propaganda'' has its roots. According to Forbes, he first wrote a story in April 1998 for Brandweek magazine about how anti-drug ads are not proven effective.

During the reporting on that piece, a man named Alan Levitt in the drug czar's ofÞce mentioned they were considering using TV shows as a vehicle for anti-drug messages instead of PSAs.

" A huge light bulb went off in my head,'' Forbes said. " I waited a year for things to unfold,'' and in April 1999, he started digging again.

When he hit pay dirt, he contacted Mediaweek, a sister publication to Brandweek. He worked on it for several months. " They were willing to publish it, but I withdrew it over that delightful catch phrase, ‘editorial differences,' '' Forbes said.

He thought of magazines like Harper's or the Atlantic Monthly, but feared getting scooped because of their long lead times. So he thought of an Internet equivalent: Salon.com. " They had the scrappy psychic wherewithal to recognize the importance of the story and not to eviscerate it,'' he said.

Forbes turned in a manuscript of 12,000 words - cut from a rough draft of 80,000 words. Wyman worked on it over Christmas vacation, paring it to fewer than 6,000 words, and putting it through a rigorous fact-checking mill. Even though the editing had some tense moments, Wyman and Forbes have high praise for each other.

Salon finally posted the story on January 13, alerted the national media and has been flying high ever since.

Now Forbes has Post-it notes plastered to his bathroom door, reminding him of key facts so he can be coherent when reporters call for interviews. He figures he's talked to about 20 so far, including an appearance on " Good Morning America.''

If it's been good for Forbes' career, the story is also good for Salon. " Stories like this create a buzz around the publication and increase our circulation,'' said David Talbot, Salon's founder and editor in chief.

Before this story, Salon's most famous scoop was that U.S. Rep. Henry Hyde had once cheated on his wife, which Salon published just as the Illinois Republican was about to lead the impeachment inquiry into President Clinton. Talbot finds Forbes' scoop sweeter.

" Even though Henry Hyde got us a lot of play, it was very controversial within media circles'' because it involved digging into a public figure's private life, he said. On the issue of the networks giving script approval to the government, though, mainstream newspapers " are unanimous in their endorsement'' of Salon's reporting, Talbot said. " The media recognizes how dangerous a precedent this can be.''
-- End Excerpt.
